messages.author: 2293944015eaac82
messages.subject: Questions - gl.grm() and gl.grm.network()
parts:
Hi everyone, 

I would like to identify clones in my dataset. I have a question about the gl.grm() and gl.grm.network(). 

I entered the R codes:
>res <- gl.grm(gl.vatrp)
>res2 <- gl.grm.network(res, gl.vatrp, relatedness_factor = 0.5)

In the genomic relationship matrix (res2), the relatedness values varied from 0.23 to 0.63. I am not sure if I understand the values clearly after reading the information in the function documentation. For those values in ~0.23, does it indicate the identity of Sibling/Parent-Offspring, and for those values 0.5 - 0.63, does it indicate the identity of twins/clones/same individual? 

I also look at the matrix in res, some of my values are negative. What does the negative mean in res? Should I determine the relatedness based on the matrix in res2 rather than res? 

Happy to hear about suggestions and insights on my analyses. Thank you very much. 

Regards,
Shan

messages.author: 592079bda2cb3220
messages.subject: Re: Questions - gl.grm() and gl.grm.network()
parts:
Hi Shan,

I recommend using a "relatedness_factor" of 0.3. Run the code below so you can get a better idea about the values of relatedness used in this function. 

Kinship estimates for pairs of individuals who share less alleles than the population average are negative, as described in the below article which is the reference mentioned in the function documentation. 
Goudet, J., Kay, T., & Weir, B. S. (2018). How to estimate kinship. Molecular Ecology, 27(20), 4121-4135.

library(dartR)
# filtering on call rate
t1 <- gl.filter.callrate(platypus.gl,threshold = 1)
# coverting to dartR object, so we can rbind individuals without messing with
# the slot ind.metrics
class(t1) <- "dartR"
# adding a replicate for testing
t1 <- rbind(t1[1,],t1)
# correcting for duplicated name
indNames(t1) <- c("replicate",indNames(platypus.gl))
#running grm
grm <- gl.grm(t1)
# Running netwrok with grm matrix
grm_plot <- gl.grm.network(grm,t1,relatedness_factor = 0.3)
# converting matrix to three columns
res_grm <- as.data.frame(as.table(grm_plot[[2]]))
# ordering from higher to lower relatedness
res_grm <- res_grm[order(res_grm$Freq,decreasing = T),]
#printing the top five pairs with higher relatedness
head(res_grm)

To identify clones, I recommend using the below code:

# Related installation instructions see:
#   https://github.com/timothyfrasier/related
library(related)
# estimating pairwise relatedness
platy_related <- gl2related(t1, save=FALSE)
res_coancestry <- coancestry(platy_related,wang=1)
# formatting of data
res_coancestry_2 <- res_coancestry$relatedness[,c(2,3,6)]
res_coancestry_3 <- cbind(res_coancestry_2$ind2.id,res_coancestry_2$ind1.id,res_coancestry_2$wang)
colnames(res_coancestry_3) <- colnames(res_coancestry_2)
res_coancestry_4 <- rbind(res_coancestry_2,res_coancestry_3)
res_coancestry_4$wang <- as.numeric(res_coancestry_4$wang)
res_coancestry_4 <- res_coancestry_4[order(res_coancestry_4$wang,decreasing = TRUE),]
head(res_coancestry_4,10)

Cheers,
Luis

parts:
Hi Shan,

It seems that your species (Vanilla trigonocarpa) is polyploid. dartR is designed to analyse diploid data. A nice article describing software to analyse polyploid data is Meirmans, Patrick G., Shenglin Liu, and Peter H. van Tienderen. "The analysis of polyploid genetic data." Journal of Heredity 109.3 (2018): 283-296.

Cheers,
Luis

messages.author: 592079bda2cb3220
messages.subject: Re: Questions - gl.grm() and gl.grm.network()
parts:
Hi Manuela,

Methods to estimate relatedness are based on the assumption that inviduals are a smaple of a large random mating population without genetic structure. Therefore, in structure populations, relatedness estimates will be biased upwards. See for example:

Wang, Jinliang. "Unbiased relatedness estimation in structured populations." Genetics 187.3 (2011): 887-901.

There is a new method that seems to solve this and another issues:

Wang, Jinliang. "Unbiased relatedness estimation in structured populations." Genetics 187.3 (2011): 887-901.

We are working in a function implementing this method in dartR.

Cheers,
Luis

Methods to estimate relatedness are based on the assumption that inviduals are a smaple of a large random mating population without genetic structure. Therefore, in structure populations, relatedness estimates will be biased upwards. See for example:

Wang, Jinliang. "Unbiased relatedness estimation in structured populations." Genetics 187.3 (2011): 887-901.

There is a new method that seems to solve this and another issues:

Wang, Jinliang. "Unbiased relatedness estimation in structured populations." Genetics 187.3 (2011): 887-901.

We are working in a function implementing this method in dartR.

Cheers,
Luis

Hi Shan,

I recommend using a "relatedness_factor" of 0.3. Run the code below so you can get a better idea about the values of relatedness used in this function. 

Kinship estimates for pairs of individuals who share less alleles than the population average are negative, as described in the below article which is the reference mentioned in the function documentation. 
Goudet, J., Kay, T., & Weir, B. S. (2018). How to estimate kinship. Molecular Ecology, 27(20), 4121-4135.

library(dartR)
# filtering on call rate
t1 <- gl.filter.callrate(platypus.gl,threshold = 1)
# coverting to dartR object, so we can rbind individuals without messing with
# the slot ind.metrics
class(t1) <- "dartR"
# adding a replicate for testing
t1 <- rbind(t1[1,],t1)
# correcting for duplicated name
indNames(t1) <- c("replicate",indNames(platypus.gl))
#running grm
grm <- gl.grm(t1)
# Running netwrok with grm matrix
grm_plot <- gl.grm.network(grm,t1,relatedness_factor = 0.3)
# converting matrix to three columns
res_grm <- as.data.frame(as.table(grm_plot[[2]]))
# ordering from higher to lower relatedness
res_grm <- res_grm[order(res_grm$Freq,decreasing = T),]
#printing the top five pairs with higher relatedness
head(res_grm)

To identify clones, I recommend using the below code:

# Related installation instructions see:
#   https://github.com/timothyfrasier/related
library(related)
# estimating pairwise relatedness
platy_related <- gl2related(t1, save=FALSE)
res_coancestry <- coancestry(platy_related,wang=1)
# formatting of data
res_coancestry_2 <- res_coancestry$relatedness[,c(2,3,6)]
res_coancestry_3 <- cbind(res_coancestry_2$ind2.id,res_coancestry_2$ind1.id,res_coancestry_2$wang)
colnames(res_coancestry_3) <- colnames(res_coancestry_2)
res_coancestry_4 <- rbind(res_coancestry_2,res_coancestry_3)
res_coancestry_4$wang <- as.numeric(res_coancestry_4$wang)
res_coancestry_4 <- res_coancestry_4[order(res_coancestry_4$wang,decreasing = TRUE),]
head(res_coancestry_4,10)

Cheers,
Luis
